mainTopic: Do the dead know what happens in this world? צדיקים are 'alive' in death and רשעים are 'dead' in life. Three stories test whether the dead know, and רבי יונתן's retraction follows.
overview: This amud continues the question of whether the dead know what happens in this world. First the גמרא explains the verse about בניהו בן יהוידע: 'son of a living man' means a צדיק is called living even after death, and the rest of the verse praises his greatness in תורה. In the mirror image, 'the dead know nothing' refers to רשעים, who are called dead even while alive, and two verses prove this. Next comes the story of the sons of רבי חייא, which leads to a distinction: the dead know their own pain but not the pain of others. The גמרא then tests that distinction with three stories: the חסיד who overheard two spirits in a cemetery, זעירי's dead innkeeper, and שמואל's visit to his dead father. Each story seems to show that the dead know, and each proof is pushed aside: maybe a newly dead person brought the news, maybe the angel דומה announces who is coming, or maybe שמואל is a special case. Finally the גמרא reports that רבי יונתן retracted his view. He himself taught that the dead talk to each other, since משה was sent to tell the אבות that God's oath had been kept. The גמרא keeps examining this proof on the next amud.

steps.title: Why call him 'son of a living man'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the wording 'בן איש חי': is everyone else the son of a dead man?
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse calls בניהו 'son of a living man.' But is everyone else a child of dead people?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is pointing out that the words 'son of a living man' seem pointless, because every person was born to a living father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every father was alive when his son was born, so calling someone 'son of a living man' adds no information. The גמרא assumes no word in פסוק is wasted. So this phrase must be teaching something special.

keyTerms.meaning: Son of a living man (a description of בניהו בן יהוידע)
Is that to say...? (introduces a challenge that sounds absurd)

phrases.english: "Son of a living man":
phrases.notes: From שמואל ב 23:20, describing בניהו בן יהוידע

phrases.english: Is that to say that everyone else
phrases.notes: A rhetorical challenge

phrases.english: are children of dead men?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא בְּנֵי מֵתֵי נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier proof, on the previous amud, that צדיקים are called living in death
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'בן איש חי' in the verse
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every person is the son of a living man, so the phrase seems superfluous.

steps.title: He is called living even in death
steps.stepSummary: The phrase means that בניהו is called 'living' even after he died.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, 'son of a living man' means that even in his death he is called living.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question. 'Living' here does not describe his father's physical life. It describes בניהו himself, who stays 'alive' forever.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'חי' is reread as a description of spiritual status, not biology. This is exactly the point the sugya needs: צדיקים are considered living even after death.

phrases.english: Rather: "son of a living man" means
that even in his death he is called living.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: בֶּן אִישׁ חַי — שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ בְּמִיתָתוֹ קָרוּי חַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of step 1
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of a word in the verse
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Living man' simply describes his father as a living person.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Living' describes the צדיק himself, who stays alive even after death.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the proof-text for the main idea of the sugya: צדיקים are called living even after death.

steps.title: He gathered many workers for תורה
steps.stepSummary: 'רב פעלים מקבצאל' is read as: he increased and gathered workers for תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Great in deeds, from קבצאל' means that he multiplied and gathered workers for the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues explaining the same verse about בניהו, phrase by phrase, as praise of his greatness in תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'פעלים' (deeds/workers) and 'קבצאל' (sounds like 'קבץ', gather) become a description of spreading תורה. He brought together many students who 'worked' at תורה.

phrases.english: "Great in deeds, from Kabze'el" means
that he multiplied and gathered workers for the Torah.
phrases.notes: A wordplay on קבצאל and קבץ

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פְּעָלִים מִקַּבְצְאֵל — שֶׁרִיבָּה וְקִבֵּץ פּוֹעֲלִים לַתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the exposition of the same verse
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בניהו spread תורה by gathering many students.

steps.title: No one like him in either Temple era
steps.stepSummary: 'He struck the two אראל of מואב' means that no one equal to him remained in the time of the מקדש ראשון or the מקדש שני.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He struck the two אראל of מואב' means that he left no one like himself, not in the era of the מקדש ראשון and not in the era of the מקדש שני.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads another phrase of the verse as praise. 'Striking the two אראל' means that he outshone everyone in both Temple periods.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The בית המקדש is called 'אריאל', so 'two אראל' hints at the two Temples. 'Struck' means he was so great that nobody in either period matched him.

keyTerms.meaning: Ariel, a name for the בית המקדש
He did not leave anyone like him

phrases.english: "And he struck the two Ariels of Moab" means
that he did not leave anyone like himself

phrases.aramaic: לֹא בְּמִקְדָּשׁ רִאשׁוֹן וְלֹא בְּמִקְדָּשׁ שֵׁנִי.
phrases.english: neither in the First Temple nor in the Second Temple.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהוּא הִכָּה אֵת שְׁנֵי אֲרִאֵל מוֹאָב — שֶׁלֹּא הִנִּיחַ כְּמוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next phrase of the same verse
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בניהו was unmatched in both Temple eras.

steps.title: The lion in the pit: breaking ice to immerse
steps.stepSummary: First opinion: 'killing the lion in the pit on a snowy day' means that he broke blocks of ice and went down to immerse.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And he went down and struck the lion in the pit on a snowy day.' Some say this means that he broke chunks of ice, went down, and immersed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last part of the verse and gives the first of two explanations. In this reading, the 'lion in the pit on a snowy day' is a brave act of טבילה in freezing water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'pit' becomes a מקוה and 'snowy day' becomes the freezing cold. 'Striking the lion' becomes his courage in breaking through the ice to purify himself.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say (introduces one of several opinions)
Blocks / chunks of ice or hail

phrases.english: "And he went down and struck the lion
inside the pit on a snowy day":
Some say:
that he broke blocks of ice,
and went down and immersed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next phrase of the same verse; opens a two-opinion explanation
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He showed great devotion by immersing in icy water.

steps.title: The lion in the pit: learning ספרא on a winter day
steps.stepSummary: Second opinion: he learned the ספרא of דבי רב on a winter day.
steps.simpleTranslation: Others say that he learned the ספרא of דבי רב on a winter's day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second explanation of the same phrase. 'Striking the lion' becomes mastering a huge body of תורה in one short winter day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the 'lion' stands for the difficult ספרא, the מדרש הלכה on ויקרא. The 'snowy day' is a short winter day. The praise is about mastery of תורה, not physical bravery.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sifra of the school of Rav, a halachic midrash on ויקרא

phrases.english: Others say:
that he learned the Sifra of the school of Rav
on a winter day.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי: דִּתְנָא סִיפְרָא דְבֵי רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: An alternative explanation of the same phrase
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He mastered the ספרא in a single winter day.
steps.whatToRemember: The whole verse about בניהו is read as praise of a צדיק whose greatness keeps him 'alive' even after death.

steps.title: The wicked are called dead while alive
steps.stepSummary: 'The dead know nothing' refers to רשעים, who are called dead even during their lives.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And the dead know nothing.' These are the wicked, who are called 'dead' even while they are alive.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to the other half of the verse in קהלת. It explains that 'the dead' who 'know nothing' are רשעים, not people who have physically died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the mirror image of the צדיקים: they are alive in death, and רשעים are dead in life. So the verse does not prove that the departed lack all awareness. It is describing the wicked.

phrases.english: "And the dead know nothing":
these are the wicked,
who even in their lifetimes are called "dead,"

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַמֵּתִים אֵינָם יוֹדְעִים מְאוּמָה — אֵלּוּ רְשָׁעִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The mirror image of step 2: צדיקים are living in death, רשעים are dead in life
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רשעים are considered dead even while alive.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'the dead know nothing' as saying that departed souls are unaware. The גמרא is reading it as a description of רשעים.

steps.title: Proof from יחזקאל: a living king called 'slain'
steps.stepSummary: Proof: יחזקאל calls a living wicked king 'חלל', a slain man.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'And you, slain wicked one, prince of Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק to prove that a living רשע can be called dead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The נביא is speaking to a king who was still alive, yet calls him 'חלל' (slain). This shows that the תנ"ך itself describes the living wicked as dead.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (introduces a proof-verse)

phrases.english: as it is said:
"And you, slain wicked one, prince of Israel".
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 21:30, addressed to a living king

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: וְאַתָּה חָלָל רָשָׁע נְשִׂיא יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves the claim of step 7
steps.raayaObject: That רשעים are called dead while alive

steps.title: Second proof: 'the dead shall be put to death'
steps.stepSummary: Alternative proof: the Torah says 'the dead shall be put to death', but he is still alive. So a רשע is considered dead from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you like, the proof comes from here: 'By the word of two witnesses or three witnesses shall the dead be put to death.' But he is alive! Rather, he was 'dead' from the beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second verse to prove the same point. It notes the strange wording, which calls a man 'dead' before he is executed, and explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse calls the condemned sinner 'המת' (the dead one) while he is still standing alive in בית דין. The only way to make sense of this is that a רשע is already considered dead.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces an alternative)
The dead shall be put to death

phrases.english: And if you wish, say it is from here:
"By the word of two witnesses
or by the word of three witnesses
shall the dead one be put to death":
phrases.notes: דברים 17:6

phrases.english: But he is alive!
phrases.notes: Pointing out the strange wording

phrases.english: Rather, he is "dead" from the outset.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second source for the same claim
steps.raayaObject: That רשעים are called dead while alive
steps.whatToRemember: צדיקים are called living even in death, and רשעים are called dead even in life. Two verses prove the second half.

steps.title: Story setup: the sons of רבי חייא forget their learning
steps.stepSummary: The sons of רבי חייא went to the villages, forgot their learning, and struggled to remember it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The sons of רבי חייא went out to the villages. Their learning became hard for them to recall, and they were pained as they tried to remember it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story. This line only sets the scene for the question that follows about whether the dead know.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sons are in distress, and their father רבי חייא has already died. This creates the real-life setting for asking whether a departed father is aware of his children's troubles.

keyTerms.meaning: Became heavy / difficult (their learning slipped away)

phrases.english: The sons of Rabbi Chiya went out to the villages.
Their learning became heavy for them (they forgot it).
They were pained trying to remember it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a story that continues the larger question of whether the dead know
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets the scene: the brothers are suffering after forgetting their learning.

steps.title: Does our father know of our pain?
steps.stepSummary: One brother asks whether their deceased father knows about their distress.
steps.simpleTranslation: One said to the other: Does our father know about this pain of ours?
steps.whatsHappening: The story's central question is asked: is the departed רבי חייא aware of his sons' suffering?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This turns the abstract sugya into a personal question. The answer will depend on how we read verses about the awareness of the dead.

phrases.english: One said to the other:
Does our father know of this pain?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises the question that the setup was building toward
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a deceased parent is aware of his children's suffering.

steps.title: How would he know? The dead do not know
steps.stepSummary: The other brother answers that their father cannot know, citing 'יכבדו בניו ולא ידע'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The other said to him: From where would he know? Isn't it written: 'His sons are honored, and he does not know'?
steps.whatsHappening: The second brother answers no, and brings a verse from איוב to show that the dead are unaware of their children's affairs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says that a dead man's children may be honored (or, as it continues, brought low) and he will not know. This seems to say that the dead have no awareness. In the next step (step 13), the other brother challenges this answer.

keyTerms.meaning: His sons are honored and he does not know (איוב 14:21)

phrases.english: The other said to him:
From where would he know?
Isn't it written:
"His sons are honored, and he does not know".
phrases.notes: איוב 14:21

steps.triggerLanguage: מְנָא יָדַע? וְהָא כְּתִיב: יִכְבְּדוּ בָנָיו וְלֹא יֵדָע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the brother's question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The dead do not know, based on איוב 14:21.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not the final word. In the continuation of the story, the other brother pushes back, so don't treat this answer as the conclusion of the sugya.

steps.title: The dead feel pain, so they must know things
steps.stepSummary: The other brother challenges the claim that the dead know nothing. He cites a פסוק in איוב and רבי יצחק's teaching that a worm hurts the dead like a needle hurts living flesh.
steps.simpleTranslation: The other brother said: Do the dead really not know anything? But it is written, 'Only his flesh upon him feels pain, and his soul upon him mourns.' And רבי יצחק said: a worm is as painful to the dead as a needle in living flesh!
steps.whatsHappening: The other brother pushes back against the answer from Step 12. He brings a פסוק showing that the dead can feel things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 said the dead do not know what happens to their children. But רבי יצחק reads the פסוק in איוב as saying the dead feel pain from worms. If the dead can feel pain, it seems they are aware, so the claim that they know nothing looks wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: but isn't it written (introduces a verse used as a challenge)

phrases.english: The other said to him:
And he does not know?
phrases.notes: Said with surprise, as a challenge.

phrases.english: But isn't it written:
"Only his flesh upon him feels pain
phrases.notes: איוב 14:22

phrases.english: and his soul upon him mourns."
And Rabbi Yitzchak said:
A worm is as painful to the dead
as a needle in living flesh!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in Step 12 that the dead do not know.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the dead know nothing (יכבדו בניו ולא ידע)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק, as explained by רבי יצחק, shows the dead feel pain. That means they have some awareness, which contradicts the idea that they know nothing.

steps.title: The dead know their own pain but not the pain of others
steps.stepSummary: The answer: the dead are aware of their own suffering, but they are not aware of what others suffer.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: about their own pain, the dead know. About the pain of others, they do not know.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the contradiction by splitting the question into two kinds of knowledge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sources can be true. The פסוק in איוב is about the dead person's own body, so he feels the worm. The פסוק 'יכבדו בניו ולא ידע' is about other people, such as his children, so he does not know what happens to them.

keyTerms.meaning: they said (the answer of the scholars)

steps.whyThisMatters: This distinction becomes the position that the rest of the sugya tests.

phrases.english: They said:
Of their own pain, they know;
of the pain of others, they do not know.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction (אוקימתא by category): own pain versus others' pain
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed the two פסוקים contradict each other about whether the dead know anything.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dead know about their own suffering only, not about what happens to others.

steps.title: A pious man sleeps in a cemetery and hears two spirits talking
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer with a ברייתא. It begins the story of a חסיד who gave charity, was scolded by his wife, slept in a cemetery, and overheard two spirits talking.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do the dead really not know about others? But a ברייתא teaches: there was a story about a חסיד who gave a dinar to a poor man on ערב ראש השנה in years of drought. His wife provoked him, so he went and slept in the cemetery. He heard two spirits talking to each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the answer from Step 14. Here it is only setting up a story that will serve as the challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'ולא? והתניא' signal that a ברייתא is about to contradict the claim that the dead do not know about others. This part only sets the scene: why the חסיד was in the cemetery and that he overheard spirits of the dead talking.

keyTerms.meaning: but wasn't it taught in a ברייתא (introduces a challenge)

steps.confusionAlert: The story is not finished here. The real point of the challenge comes later in the story, so keep following it.

phrases.english: And they don't? But wasn't it taught:
An incident with a certain pious man
who gave a dinar to a poor man
on the eve of Rosh Hashanah
in years of drought,
and his wife provoked him,
and he went and slept in the cemetery.
And he heard two spirits
talking to each other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the distinction made in Step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the dead do not know about the pain of others
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא describes spirits of the dead who are aware of what is happening in the world. That suggests the dead do know things beyond their own pain.

steps.title: First year: the spirit learns that hail will strike the early sowing
steps.stepSummary: One spirit cannot leave because she was buried in a reed mat. The other goes, listens from behind the heavenly curtain, and reports that hail will strike whoever sows in the first rainfall. The חסיד sows in the second rainfall, and only his crop is saved.
steps.simpleTranslation: One spirit said to her friend: Come, let us roam the world and hear from behind the curtain what disaster is coming to the world. Her friend said: I cannot, because I am buried in a mat of reeds. You go and tell me what you hear. She went, roamed, and came back. Her friend asked what she heard. She said: Whoever sows in the first rainfall will be struck by hail. The חסיד sowed in the second rainfall. Everyone else's crops were struck, but his were not.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. The spirits learn about a coming disaster in the world, and the living חסיד uses what he overheard to save his crop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The spirits are clearly interested in, and aware of, what will happen to living people in the world. That already pushes against the idea that the dead know only about themselves. The חסיד's success shows that what the spirits heard was true.

phrases.english: One said to her friend:
My friend, come, let us roam the world,
and let us hear from behind the curtain
what calamity is coming to the world.
Her friend said to her: I cannot,
for I am buried in a mat of reeds.
Rather, you go,
and whatever you hear, tell me.
She went, roamed, and came back.
And her friend said to her:
My friend, what did you hear from behind the curtain?
She said to her: I heard
that anyone who sows in the first rainfall
hail will strike him.
He went and sowed in the second rainfall.
The crops of the whole world were struck,
his were not struck.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרָה חֲדָא לַחֲבֶרְתָּהּ: חֲבֶרְתִּי, בּוֹאִי וְנָשׁוּט בָּעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא that was opened as a challenge in Step 15.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead are aware of events in the world of the living
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of the חסיד in the cemetery

steps.title: Second year: the spirit learns that blight will strike the late sowing
steps.stepSummary: The next year the חסיד returns to the cemetery and hears the same conversation. This time the spirit reports that blight will strike whoever sows in the second rainfall. He sows in the first rainfall, and again only his crop is spared.
steps.simpleTranslation: The next year he went and slept in the cemetery again and heard the same two spirits talking. One said: Come, let us roam and hear from behind the curtain what disaster is coming. The other said: Didn't I already tell you I cannot, because I am buried in a mat of reeds? You go, then come and tell me. She went, roamed, and returned. Asked what she heard, she said: Whoever sows in the second rainfall will be struck by blight. He sowed in the first rainfall. Everyone else's crops were blighted, but his were not.
steps.whatsHappening: The story repeats with a new year and a new disaster. Again the חסיד uses the spirits' information to protect his crop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The repetition confirms that the spirits regularly learn about the future of the living world, and that their information keeps coming true. This builds the pattern that the next part of the story will use to finish the challenge against Step 14.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two years. In year one the danger was hail on the first rainfall, so he sowed late. In year two the danger was blight on the second rainfall, so he sowed early.

phrases.english: The next year
he went and slept in the cemetery,
and he heard those two spirits
talking with each other.
One said to her friend:
Come, let us roam the world
and hear from behind the curtain
what calamity is coming to the world.
She said to her: My friend,
didn't I already tell you:

phrases.aramaic: אֵינִי יְכוֹלָה שֶׁאֲנִי קְבוּרָה בְּמַחְצֶלֶת שֶׁל קָנִים?!
phrases.english: I cannot, for I am buried in a mat of reeds?!
Rather, you go,

phrases.aramaic: וּמַה שֶּׁאַתְּ שׁוֹמַעַת בּוֹאִי וְאִמְרִי לִי.
phrases.english: and whatever you hear, come and tell me.
She went, roamed, and came back.
And her friend said to her:
My friend, what did you hear from behind the curtain?
She said to her: I heard
that anyone who sows in the second rainfall
blight will strike him.
He went and sowed in the first rainfall.
The crops of the whole world were blighted
and his were not blighted.

steps.triggerLanguage: לַשָּׁנָה הָאַחֶרֶת הָלַךְ וְלָן בְּבֵית הַקְּבָרוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the pattern of Step 16 in a second year with a different disaster.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead are aware of events in the world of the living
steps.raayaSupportSource: The continuation of the ברייתא of the חסיד

steps.title: The wife learns the secret and uses it in a quarrel
steps.stepSummary: The חסיד's wife asks why only his crops survived two years in a row. He tells her the whole story. Later, during a fight, she insults the dead girl's mother by mentioning the reed mat.
steps.simpleTranslation: His wife said to him: Why is it that last year everyone's crops were struck and yours were not, and now everyone's crops were blighted and yours were not? He told her the whole story. They said: Only a few days later a fight broke out between the wife of that חסיד and the mother of that girl. She said to her: Go, and I will show you your daughter, who is buried in a mat of reeds.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. It explains how the spirits' private conversation got out into the world of the living.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חסיד tells his wife, and she uses the secret about the reed mat to insult the girl's mother. Now the living know what the spirits said privately. This sets up the next scene, where the spirits find out that their words have spread.
steps.confusionAlert: The girl's mother is alive. The insult is about her dead daughter, who was buried in a cheap reed mat instead of proper shrouds. That is the detail the spirit mentioned in step 16.

phrases.english: His wife said to him:
Why is it that last year
the crops of the whole world were struck
and yours were not struck,

phrases.aramaic: וְעַכְשָׁיו שֶׁל כָּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ נִשְׁדַּף
phrases.english: and now the crops of the whole world were blighted
and yours were not blighted?
He told her all these things.
phrases.notes: Now the secret has reached the living.

phrases.english: They said: Not even a few days passed
before a quarrel broke out
between the wife of that pious man
and the mother of that young girl.
She said to her: Go, and I will show you your daughter,
who is buried in a mat of reeds.
phrases.notes: An insult, since a reed mat was a shameful burial.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא story by explaining how the spirits' secret reached the living.
steps.raayaObject: Sets up the claim that the dead know what the living say and do.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of the חסיד in the cemetery.

steps.title: The spirits know they were overheard, so the dead know
steps.stepSummary: In the third year, the second spirit refuses to go out, because their private words were already heard among the living. The גמרא concludes that the dead know what happens in this world.
steps.simpleTranslation: The next year he went and slept in the cemetery again, and he heard those spirits talking to each other. One said to the other: My friend, come, let us roam the world and hear from behind the curtain what disaster is coming to the world. She answered: My friend, leave me alone. The words between me and you have already been heard among the living. So we see that the dead know.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends, and the גמרא draws its conclusion: the dead do know what the living are doing. This finishes the challenge that began in step 15.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 14 the answer was that the dead feel their own pain but do not know about others. Here the spirit knows that the living repeated her private words. That looks like knowledge of the living world, which contradicts step 14.
steps.whatToRemember: The ending 'אלמא ידעי' turns the whole חסיד story into a challenge against the answer in step 14.

phrases.english: The following year he went
and slept in the cemetery
and heard those same spirits
talking with each other.
One said to the other: My friend,
come, let us roam the world
and hear from behind the curtain
what disaster is coming to the world.
She said to her: My friend, leave me alone,
the words that were between me and you
have already been heard among the living.
Apparently, the dead know.
phrases.notes: The גמרא's conclusion, aimed against the answer in step 14.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the story and draws the inference that the dead know about the living.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead know what goes on in the world of the living.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The spirit's statement in the ברייתא that their words were already heard among the living.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 14, that the dead do not know about others.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The spirit knew what the living were saying, so the dead do know about others.

steps.title: Maybe a newly dead person told them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. Perhaps someone who heard the gossip died and told the spirits what was being said.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps another person died, went there, and told them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back against the proof from the חסיד story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The spirits did not have to see the living world themselves. A person who heard the quarrel could have died and brought the news to the cemetery. If so, the dead learn news only through new arrivals, and step 14's answer still stands.

phrases.english: Perhaps another person died,
and went and told them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference drawn in step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from the חסיד story, not the question itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The spirits could have learned the news from someone who died later, not by knowing it themselves.

steps.title: זעירי's dead innkeeper tells him where his money is
steps.stepSummary: A new proof: זעירי's innkeeper died while holding his money. At her grave she told him where it was and sent a message to her mother through a woman who would die the next day. So the dead know.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: זעירי used to leave his coins with his innkeeper. While he was going back and forth to the study hall of רב, she died. He went after her to the cemetery and said to her: Where are the coins? She told him: Go and take them from under the hinge of the door in such-and-such a place. And tell my mother to send me my comb and my tube of eye-paint with such-and-such a woman, who is coming here tomorrow. So we see that the dead know!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new story, opened with 'תא שמע', to challenge step 14's answer again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dead innkeeper knows that a certain living woman will die and arrive tomorrow. No newly dead person could have told her that, so the rejection in step 20 does not work here. The גמרא concludes again: the dead do know about the living world.

keyTerms.meaning: זעירי, an אמורא and student of רב

steps.confusionAlert: Her knowing where the money is hidden is not the real proof, since she hid it herself while alive. The key is that she knows which living woman will die and come tomorrow.
steps.whyThisMatters: This story avoids the weakness of the חסיד proof, because no one who died earlier could have brought this news.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Ze'iri used to deposit coins
with his innkeeper.
While he was coming and going to Rav's study hall,
she died.
phrases.notes: He did not know where she had put the money.

phrases.english: He went after her to the cemetery,
he said to her: Where are the coins?
She said to him: Go take them
from under the hinge of the door
in such-and-such a place,
and tell my mother
to send me my comb
and my tube of eye-paint
with such-and-such a woman who is coming tomorrow.
phrases.notes: She knows who will die tomorrow.

phrases.english: Apparently, the dead know!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: דִּזְעֵירִי הֲוָה מַפְקֵיד זוּזֵי גַּבֵּי אוּשְׁפִּיזְכָתֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof was rejected in step 20, the גמרא brings a new proof for the same challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 14, that the dead do not know what happens to others.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The dead innkeeper knew a living woman would die tomorrow. No dead messenger could have told her this, so the dead must know about the living world.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead know what happens among the living.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of זעירי and his innkeeper.

steps.title: Maybe the angel announces who is coming
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from זעירי's innkeeper. Perhaps the angel דומה announces to the dead ahead of time who will die, so they do not actually know on their own.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps דומה comes first and announces it to them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the last proof. Maybe the innkeeper knew the woman would die tomorrow only because an angel told the dead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The innkeeper's knowledge does not prove that the dead watch the living world. Information about upcoming arrivals could come from דומה, the angel in charge of the dead. That is a narrow, outside source, not general awareness.

keyTerms.meaning: The angel in charge of the souls of the dead

phrases.english: Perhaps Duma comes beforehand
phrases.notes: דומה is the angel over the dead.

phrases.english: and announces to them.
phrases.notes: He announces who will arrive tomorrow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from זעירי's innkeeper in step 21.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof. It does not claim the dead do not know.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The innkeeper's knowledge of a coming death can be explained by an angel's announcement rather than by the dead knowing on their own.

steps.title: שמואל's father dies holding orphans' money
steps.stepSummary: A new proof begins. שמואל's father held orphans' money and died while שמואל was away. Nobody knew where the money was, so people called שמואל 'son of the one who ate orphans' money.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: People would deposit orphans' money with שמואל's father. When he died, שמואל was not with him. People called שמואל: 'Son of the one who eats orphans' money.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new proof with a story. This step sets up the problem that sends שמואל to the cemetery.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The background matters. Only the dead father knows where the money is. That is why שמואל must go speak with the dead, which sets the stage for what the dead turn out to know.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear. Introduces a new proof.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
that with Shmuel's father
they would deposit with him
the money of orphans.
When he died,
Shmuel was not with him.
phrases.notes: So שמואל never learned where the money was.

phrases.english: They would call him:
'Son of the one who eats orphans' money.'

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: דַּאֲבוּהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל הֲווֹ קָא מַפְקְדִי גַּבֵּיהּ זוּזֵי דְיַתְמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from זעירי's innkeeper was rejected in step 22, the גמרא opens a third 'תא שמע' story to challenge step 14's answer again.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead know what happens in this world
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of שמואל and his father

steps.title: שמואל searches the cemetery for his father
steps.stepSummary: שמואל goes to the cemetery and asks for 'אבא.' He has to become more specific, ending with 'אבא בר אבא, the father of שמואל.' The dead tell him his father went up to the heavenly ישיבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went after him to the cemetery. He said: 'I want אבא.' They said: 'There are many people named אבא here.' He said: 'I want אבא בר אבא.' They said: 'There are also many people named אבא בר אבא here.' He said: 'I want אבא בר אבא, the father of שמואל. Where is he?' They said: 'He went up to the ישיבה on high.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. שמואל keeps narrowing down which dead person he wants until the dead tell him where his father is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is story detail that moves the plot forward. The key proof has not come yet. It also shows that שמואל's father was a righteous person who studies in the heavenly ישיבה.

phrases.english: He went after him to the cemetery.
He said to them: I want Abba!
phrases.notes: אבא was his father's name.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: אַבָּא טוּבָא אִיכָּא הָכָא.
phrases.english: They said to him: There are many Abbas here.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: בָּעֵינָא אַבָּא בַּר אַבָּא.
phrases.english: He said to them: I want Abba bar Abba.
They said to him:

phrases.aramaic: אַבָּא בַּר אַבָּא נָמֵי טוּבָא אִיכָּא הָכָא.
phrases.english: There are also many Abba bar Abbas here.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: בָּעֵינָא אַבָּא בַּר אַבָּא
phrases.english: He said to them: I want Abba bar Abba,
the father of Shmuel. Where is he?
They said to him: He went up to the yeshiva on high.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story that serves as the proof.

steps.title: לוי is kept outside the heavenly ישיבה
steps.stepSummary: שמואל sees his friend לוי sitting outside. לוי explains he is being kept out because, in life, he skipped רבי אפס's ישיבה for years and hurt רבי אפס's feelings.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meanwhile, he saw לוי sitting outside. He said to him: 'Why are you sitting outside? Why didn't you go up?' He said: 'Because they tell me: For all those years that you did not go up to the yeshiva of רבי אפס and upset him, we will not let you into the heavenly yeshiva.'
steps.whatsHappening: A side story inside the main story. שמואל meets לוי, who is being kept out of the heavenly ישיבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This detail is not part of the proof itself. It teaches how seriously Heaven treats hurting the feelings of a teacher of תורה. It also sets up how שמואל will later help לוי.

keyTerms.meaning: לוי, a sage and friend of שמואל
The head of the yeshiva in his time

phrases.english: Meanwhile, he saw Levi
sitting outside.
He said to him: Why are you sitting outside?
Why did you not go up?
He said to him: Because they tell me:
for all those years
that you did not go up to the yeshiva of Rabbi Afes
and upset him,
we will not let you into the yeshiva on high.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side episode within the ongoing proof story.

steps.title: The father cries and laughs
steps.stepSummary: שמואל's father arrives crying and laughing. He cries because שמואל will join him soon, and he laughs because שמואל is very important in this world. שמואל uses his importance to get לוי admitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meanwhile his father came. He saw that he was crying and laughing. He said to him: 'Why are you crying?' He said: 'Because you are coming here soon.' 'Why are you laughing?' 'Because you are very important in this world.' He said: 'If I am important, let them bring לוי in.' And they brought לוי in.
steps.whatsHappening: The father appears and reveals that שמואל will soon die. This is the key detail for the proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father knows something about the future of a living person: that שמואל will die soon. He also knows שמואל's standing in this world. The story then shows שמואל's importance in action, since לוי is admitted.
steps.confusionAlert: Remember 'soon' (לַעֲגָל) here. Since שמואל did not die the very next day, דומה's announcement about who dies tomorrow cannot explain how the father knew. That is what makes this proof stronger than the previous one.

phrases.english: Meanwhile his father came,
and he saw that he was crying and laughing.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי טַעְמָא קָא בָכֵית?
phrases.english: He said to him: Why are you crying?
He said to him: Because you are coming here soon.
Why are you laughing?
Because you are very important in this world.
He said to him: If I am important,
let them bring Levi in.
And they brought Levi in.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the central figure of the proof into the story and reveals the key fact.

steps.title: Where the orphans' money is hidden
steps.stepSummary: The father tells שמואל the money is in the millhouse. Their own money is on the top and bottom, and the orphans' money is in the middle. That way thieves or rot would harm only the family's money.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: 'Where is the orphans' money?' He said: 'Go take it from the millhouse. The top and bottom are ours, and the middle is the orphans'.' He said: 'Why did you do that?' He said: 'If thieves steal, they will steal from ours. If the earth eats it, it will eat from ours.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story's original problem is solved. שמואל learns where the money is, and the father explains his careful arrangement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father protected the orphans by putting his own money in the risky spots. Thieves take from the top, and dampness in the earth damages the bottom. This clears the family's name, but the proof itself comes from the earlier 'you are coming soon.'

keyTerms.meaning: The top ones and the bottom ones
The earth consumes it (rot or damage)

phrases.english: He said to him: Where is the orphans' money?
He said to him: Go take it
from the millhouse.
The top and bottom are ours,
and the middle is the orphans'.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי טַעְמָא עֲבַדְתְּ הָכִי?
phrases.english: He said to him: Why did you do this?
He said to him: If thieves steal,
they will steal from ours.
phrases.notes: Thieves take from the top first.

phrases.english: If the earth consumes it,
it will consume from ours.
phrases.notes: Damage from the ground hits the bottom layer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the problem from step 23 and completes the story.

steps.title: So the dead know
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws its conclusion: the dead know what happens in this world. The father knew שמואל would die soon, and דומה's next-day announcement cannot explain that.
steps.simpleTranslation: So we see that they know!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states what the story proves: the dead have knowledge of this world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous rejection said דומה announces who will die the next day. שמואל did not die the next day, yet his father already knew he would come 'soon.' So the earlier excuse does not work here (as תוספות explains).

keyTerms.meaning: So we see, it follows. Introduces a conclusion.

phrases.english: So we see that they know!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the inference from the story of שמואל's father. It renews the challenge against step 14's answer and gets around the rejection in step 22, because שמואל did not die the next day.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead know what happens in this world
steps.raayaSupportSource: The father's knowledge that שמואל would soon die, which goes beyond a next-day announcement

steps.title: שמואל is a special case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. שמואל is unusually important, so Heaven may announce his coming long in advance by telling the dead to make room for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps שמואל is different. Since he is important, they announce ahead of time: 'Make room!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down this proof as well. The father's knowledge may come from a special announcement made only for an important person like שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This rejection extends the דומה idea. For ordinary people the announcement comes the day before, but for someone as great as שמואל it may come much earlier. So the story still does not prove that the dead know on their own.
steps.whatToRemember: Two proofs (זעירי's innkeeper and שמואל's father) are both rejected the same way. The dead may know only what Heaven announces to them, either the day before or, for a great person, much earlier.

phrases.english: Perhaps Shmuel is different,
since he is important,
they announce ahead of time: Make room!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the conclusion drawn in step 28.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from שמואל's father.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: שמואל is an exceptional case. An early heavenly announcement for an important person explains the father's knowledge without showing that the dead know on their own.

steps.title: Even רבי יונתן changed his mind
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא states that רבי יונתן, who had said the dead know nothing, later took back that view.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even רבי יונתן changed his mind.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes a short claim that רבי יונתן later retracted his earlier opinion. This line sets up the next step, which brings the proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רבי יונתן seemed to say that the dead are unaware of this world. The גמרא now says he did not keep that view. The evidence will come from another teaching in his own name.

keyTerms.meaning: He went back on his view, changed his mind

steps.confusionAlert: This line is a claim, not the proof. The proof comes in the next step.

phrases.english: And even Rabbi Yonatan changed his mind,
phrases.notes: He had earlier taught that the dead know nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from שמואל's father was rejected, the גמרא adds that רבי יונתן himself retracted his earlier view.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי יונתן did not keep his view that the dead know nothing.

steps.title: רבי יונתן's own teaching that the dead talk to each other
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני quotes רבי יונתן deriving from a פסוק that the dead converse with each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: From where do we know that the dead talk with each other? Because it says: 'And ה' said to him: This is the land that I swore to אברהם, to יצחק, and to יעקב, saying.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the proof that רבי יונתן changed his mind. He himself taught that the dead speak with one another, and he quotes a פסוק as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the dead can talk to each other, they can learn and share information. That does not fit the view that the dead know nothing. The key word in the פסוק is לאמר, which will be explained next.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know? (asks for a source)
As it is said (introduces a פסוק)

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן:
phrases.english: As Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan:

phrases.aramaic: מִנַּיִן לַמֵּתִים שֶׁמְסַפְּרִים זֶה עִם זֶה —
phrases.english: From where do we know that the dead talk with each other?
As it says: "And ה׳ said to him (Moshe):
This is the land that I swore
to Avraham, to Yitzchak, and to Yaakov, saying."
phrases.notes: דברים 34:4. The extra word לאמר ('saying') is the key.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the evidence for the claim in step 30.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יונתן retracted his view that the dead know nothing.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יונתן's own teaching, from the פסוק in דברים ל"ד, that the dead talk with each other.

steps.title: What does the word 'saying' mean here?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the word לאמר adds to the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'saying' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about the extra word לאמר in the פסוק. This question sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually לאמר means 'saying the following.' Here no further speech follows, so the word seems extra. The גמרא wants to know what message is being sent and to whom.

keyTerms.meaning: What is? What does it mean?

phrases.english: What does "saying" mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Focuses on the key word in the פסוק just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the extra word לאמר.

steps.title: משה is sent to tell the אבות the oath was kept
steps.stepSummary: לאמר means that הקב"ה told משה to go tell the אבות that the promise to them was kept for their children.
steps.simpleTranslation: הקב"ה said to משה: Go tell them, אברהם, יצחק and יעקב: The oath I swore to you, I have already kept for your children.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that לאמר is a message משה must bring to the dead אבות. Since משה would deliver it after his own death, this shows that the dead speak with each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The אבות had died long before. משה was about to die. Telling him to pass on a message to them means the dead can hear and talk. This shows that רבי יונתן did not really hold that the dead are cut off from all knowledge.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy One, Blessed is He
I have kept it, fulfilled it

steps.whatToRemember: In the end, even רבי יונתן agrees that the dead can talk to each other and can be told what happens in this world. משה was sent to tell the אבות that the promise of ארץ ישראל was kept.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that even רבי יונתן accepts that the dead converse and can receive messages about this world. It does not settle the whole question: the גמרא keeps examining this proof on the next amud.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed is He, said to Moshe:
Go and tell them,
Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov:
The oath that I swore to you
I have already kept for your children.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 32 and completes the proof of step 31.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: לאמר means משה is to bring a message to the dead אבות, which shows that the dead talk and can receive information.
